Asking for, Recording and Passing on Information
In the workplace, it is important to ask for, record and pass on information in meetings.
When you ask for information, you can use Wh- questions.
When recording information, you use short phrases. For example, extremely high winds.
When you pass on information, you report on what another person has said. You don't normally use the speaker's exact words (direct speech) but reported (indirect) speech. You use "reporting" verbs.

What does this weather forecast say?
They said that the storm would reach the city tomorrow.
In English, sometimes we need to interrupt people. This can be because we need to say something, express our opinion, or make a suggestion.
Interruptions are acceptable and perfectly normal, but too many interruptions can seem rude. Here are some common ways we can use to interrupt:

{"rows":2,"columns":1,"cells":["{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \" Interrupting Politely\"}","{\"type\": \"text\", \"content\": \"
  • Sorry to interrupt ...
  • Excuse me, but ...
  • Pardon me, ...
  • Er, well ...
  • Can I add/ask something here?
\"}"],"styles":" intro_table_border instruction_table_background"}

Examples:
  • Sorry to interrupt, but I missed that last part.
  • Er, well, I live a bit far from here.
The verb “interrupt” follows the pattern “interrupt someone”. We do not use any prepositions after this verb.

Example:
  • She tried to explain the problem, but he interrupted her mid-sentence.
a statement telling someone that bad weather may happen in the future
Example: There is an extreme weather warning for today.
These are words you use when talking about the weather.
to increase in amount and speed
Example: There will be strong winds, possibly gusting up to 100 km an hour.
Example: Torrential rains are in the forecast.
a sudden flood of water caused by heavy rain
Example: There is a possibility of a flash flood.
a violent tropical storm in which strong winds move in a circle
Example: We haven't had a cyclone for decades.
moving air that is strong enough to cause damage
Example: The forecast calls for extremely high winds.
Example: The severe storm will not reach the city.

images.text:
Janet: Alright everyone. As you are probably aware, there is an extreme weather warning for today. I just wanted to go over our game plan if we run into an emergency. Miranda, would you take notes please?
Miranda: Certainly.
Peter: Excuse me, but wouldn't it be wiser to just work from home?
Janet: Unfortunately we have several urgent meetings scheduled. According to the weather forecast, this severe storm will most likely not reach the city.

Renata: Sorry to interrupt, but can I ask something here? What kind of storm are we anticipating?
Peter: A cyclone. We haven't had a cyclone for decades. Extremely strong winds, possibly
gusting up to 63 miles an hour. Torrential rains will accompany it, no doubt. Possibly a flash flood.
Miranda: Pardon me? Am I to write that down? What exactly was the forecast?
Janet: Extremely high winds. Please record that.
Miranda: Got it, thanks.

Janet: The secretary told me she will keep us posted via email and I will personally visit each office in the event of an emergency. Does anyone travel far ...
Renata: Er, well, I live in Megville.
Miranda: Renata, I'm ten minutes away. Come over until the weather improves. Worst case scenario, you can always stay at my place!
Renata: Thanks Miranda. I hope I won't need to take you up on that.
Miranda: Renata at Miranda's in emergency - I've recorded that!
Janet: Alright everyone. Let's get to work and hope for the best!
